questions.q: To reason about who controls the Internet, it helps to compare it with other large-scale infrastructure such as roads, railroads and waterways. What does that comparison suggest shapes how such infrastructure is run?
choices: A single national government that owns and operates the whole system
Governance at regional, state, national and international levels; standards set by standards organizations; and a role for industry, user groups and non-profits
Only the private companies that own the physical equipment
Only an international treaty body such as the United Nations
questions.explain: A river crossing towns, states and countries involves governments at several levels. Roads need standards such as lane widths and on-ramp designs, which standards organizations set. Industry and user groups also play a part. The Internet has all three kinds of influence.

questions.q: Many groups (governments, businesses, users, standards bodies, civil society) each want a say in how the Internet is governed, and they don't all want compatible things. What is this kind of setting or governance model called? (one word, hyphen optional)
questions.explain: Internet governance happens largely in a multistakeholder setting: many actors who care about the outcome take part in decisions, even though their interests may conflict.

questions.q: In the 2002 paper "Tussle in Cyberspace: Defining Tomorrow's Internet," David Clark and colleagues introduced the term "tussle." What does it describe?
choices: Contention between packets competing for bandwidth on a shared link
A billing dispute between two ISPs over peering fees
Stakeholders whose interests may be adverse to each other each fighting for their own favored interests
The handshake two routers perform before exchanging routes
questions.explain: In Clark et al.'s terms, the tussle is the conflict among Internet stakeholders with opposing interests, each pushing for what it favors. It is a social and political process, not a technical mechanism.

questions.q: Clark et al. argue that the tussle among Internet stakeholders is a harmful side effect that good governance should try to eliminate.
questions.explain: They argue the opposite: the tussle among stakeholders is crucial to the evolution of the Internet.

questions.q: Which of the following really do have a hand in controlling the Internet?
choices: Internet users
Internet service providers
Nation states (countries)
The United Nations
Internet equipment manufacturers
One central authority that has the final say over the whole Internet
questions.explain: Control is spread across users, ISPs, countries, the UN, standards bodies such as the IETF, equipment manufacturers and non-profits. No single entity controls everything, which is why the honest answer is "it's really complicated."

questions.q: Because the Internet is a network of networks made up of hundreds of millions of individually operated networks, each operator has some autonomy over what it does within its own part of the Internet.
questions.explain: Each network operator makes its own local decisions. That is one reason there is no simple answer to who controls the Internet.

questions.q: Which governance role most clearly needs to be global rather than left to each country?
choices: Deciding which content citizens may access
Setting the technical aspects of the Internet, such as its addressing scheme
Deciding local laws about online speech
Choosing which websites to filter at a national boundary
questions.explain: As Bob Kahn puts it, each government will make its own decisions for its own country, but the technical aspects need global oversight. Every country can't invent its own addressing scheme and still expect everything to work. Content rules, in contrast, are often set by national or local governments within their own jurisdictions.

questions.q: The reference model for discussing Internet governance has three layers. What are they, from bottom to top?
choices: Infrastructure layer; names and numbers; content layer
Physical; network; application
Names and numbers; infrastructure layer; content layer
Content layer; infrastructure layer; names and numbers
questions.explain: The bottom layer is infrastructure (technical standards), the middle is names and numbers (Internet names and addresses), and the top is content (policy and social processes).

questions.q: The three-layer governance reference model (infrastructure, names/numbers, content) is just another way of drawing the Internet/OSI protocol stack.
questions.explain: This model is explicitly different from the Internet/OSI protocol stack. It is a framework for breaking down governance questions, not a way of organizing protocols.

questions.q: How does the nature of the issues change as you move up the governance reference model from the infrastructure layer to the content layer?
choices: From social and policy issues to purely technical ones
From national issues to purely local ones
From primarily technical issues to primarily social, policy and governance issues
From software issues to hardware issues
questions.explain: The infrastructure layer is about technical standards. Names and numbers mixes technical standards with social processes. The content layer is mainly a matter of social processes, policy and governance.

questions.q: Deciding which organization gets to match the name www.umass.edu with the University of Massachusetts Amherst falls under which governance layer?
choices: Infrastructure layer
Names and numbers
Content layer
None; it is handled automatically by the transport layer
questions.explain: The names-and-numbers layer covers Internet names (such as www.umass.edu) and Internet addresses (such as 128.119.40.186), including who assigns them.

questions.q: In the governance reference model, which layer covers standardizing a data format such as mp4?
choices: Content layer
Names and numbers
Infrastructure layer
It falls outside the model
questions.explain: The infrastructure layer covers technical standards for hardware (links, switches, routers), for protocols and message formats, and for data formats such as mp4. The content layer is about what content is allowed and how it is regulated, not how it is encoded.

questions.q: Which of these issues belong to the content layer of the governance model?
choices: Intellectual property
Defining, filtering and regulating content
Standards for links, switches and routers
Assigning IP addresses to hosts
Protocol message formats
questions.explain: The content layer covers policy and social processes such as intellectual property and how content is defined, filtered and regulated. Hardware standards and message formats belong to the infrastructure layer. Address assignment belongs to names and numbers.

questions.q: Which description best fits the names-and-numbers layer?
choices: Purely technical standards, with no social or governance dimension
Technical standards together with social and governance processes for Internet names and addresses
Purely policy decisions, with no technical component
Hardware standards for links and routers
questions.explain: Names and numbers sits in the middle. Part of it is technical, such as how names are translated to addresses. Part of it is social and governance work, such as who gets which name and how disputes are resolved.

questions.q: Which of these organizations work mainly at the infrastructure layer, setting technical standards?
choices: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)
Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
Internet Governance Forum (IGF)
National governments
questions.explain: The IETF (Internet protocols), 3GPP (cellular) and IEEE (Ethernet and Wi-Fi) set technical standards. The IGF and national governments are players at the content layer.

questions.q: What is the main reason standards are needed?
choices: To make each vendor's products deliberately incompatible with its competitors'
Interoperability and interconnectability: so separately built products and systems can work together
To let governments tax equipment
To guarantee that only one company makes each product
questions.explain: A device plugs in and works anywhere in the U.S. because the electrical system there is standardized. Without shared standards, separately built systems can't connect or work together.

questions.q: How many different plug standards are there worldwide (the reason a U.S. device often won't plug in abroad)?
questions.explain: There are 15 plug standards worldwide (plus both 110V and 220V systems). With that many, it's hard to call any one of them "the" standard, and devices don't work across regions.

questions.q: Tony Ralston wrote that as a society becomes more complex and industrial, it becomes necessary for what to "fit together and to interoperate"?
choices: Only its machines and electrical devices
Its products, processes and procedures
Only its communication networks
Its national governments
questions.explain: Ralston names products, processes and procedures, so not just technology. He adds that this interoperation integrates society further, which in turn increases social interdependency and complexity.

questions.q: In 1860, how many different railroad track gauges were in use in the United States?
questions.explain: In 1860, 20 different gauges (the distance between the two rails) were in use, including 4'8.5", 4'9", 5'0", 5'6" and 6'0".

questions.q: What was the practical consequence of having many different track gauges in the 1860s U.S.?
choices: Trains could only run at night
A train built for one rail system couldn't run on another, so no single train could travel end to end across the country
Each railroad had to buy its own telegraph network
Passenger and freight trains had to share the same cars
questions.explain: The separate rail systems couldn't interoperate. Imagine an Internet packet that couldn't travel from one end of the Internet to the other.

questions.q: What single national track gauge standard had U.S. railroads adopted by 1886?
choices: 5 ft 0 in
6 ft 0 in
4 ft 8.5 in
5 ft 6 in
questions.explain: By 1886 the U.S. had one 4 ft 8.5 in standard gauge, so separate railroads could interconnect and one train could cross many of their networks.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes how U.S. railroads reached a single standard gauge?
choices: 1862: the U.S. government convenes major railroad owners to discuss standards; 1867: 29 railroad companies form the Master Car Builders Association; 1886: the 4'8.5" standard gauge is adopted
1862: Congress mandates a single gauge by law; 1867: all railroads are nationalized; 1886: private railroads are restored
1862: the ITU publishes a railroad gauge standard; 1886: U.S. railroads adopt it
1867: one railroad buys out all the others and imposes its gauge
questions.explain: Government convened the industry, the industry formed its own standardization body (the Master Car Builders Association), and a common standard followed. Government and industry each played a part, which is again a multistakeholder pattern.

questions.q: How does the railroad gauge story map onto the Internet?
choices: The Internet is one network run by a single operator, like a nationalized railroad
Many individually owned networks interconnect into a network of networks, and common standards let them interoperate so a packet, like a train, can travel end to end
Every network on the Internet uses a different addressing scheme, just as railroads kept different gauges
Railroads and the Internet both avoided standards and relied on adapters
questions.explain: Standard gauge let separate railway networks interconnect and act as one system. In the same way, Internet standards let independently operated networks form a network of networks that a packet can cross end to end.

questions.q: Bob Kahn, one of the fathers of the Internet, calls himself a pragmatist about Internet control. What does he say needs global oversight?
choices: What content each country's citizens may view
Nothing; each country should decide everything for itself
The evolution of the Internet's technical aspects, because every country can't come up with a different addressing scheme and expect everything to work
The pricing of domain names
questions.explain: Kahn expects each government to make its own decisions according to its own culture and style. The technical aspects, such as addressing, still need a common global standard.

questions.q: Which organization describes itself as "a large open international community of network designers, operators, vendors, and researchers concerned with the evolution of the Internet architecture and the smooth operation of the Internet"?
choices: ICANN
Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
Internet Governance Forum (IGF)
questions.explain: That is the IETF's self-description. Its list of designers, operators, vendors and researchers is itself a multistakeholder community. The IETF oversees the technical evolution of the Internet.

questions.q: What are the IETF documents that define the Internet's technical standards, such as IP, TCP, UDP and HTTP, called?
questions.explain: The IETF publishes standards as Requests for Comments (RFCs). There are more than 9000 so far, and they keep being updated.

questions.q: Which phrase characterizes the IETF's standards process?
choices: "One country, one vote"
"Rough consensus and running code"
"Move fast and break things"
"Top-down mandates from a governing board"
questions.explain: The IETF works through working groups and open meetings held twice a year. Its decisions rest on "rough consensus and running code": broad agreement backed by implementations that actually work.

questions.q: The IETF develops standards in working groups and holds open meetings twice a year.
questions.explain: Working groups do the standards work, and the twice-yearly IETF meetings are open to many stakeholders.

questions.q: Which of these protocols are standardized by the IETF in RFCs?
choices: IP (Internet Protocol)
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)
UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi
4G LTE cellular
questions.explain: IP, TCP, UDP and HTTP are all defined in IETF RFCs. IEEE standardizes Wi-Fi (802.11), and 3GPP sets the 4G LTE specifications.

questions.q: RFC 791 is an example of an IETF technical standard. What does it define?
choices: The Wi-Fi link-layer protocol
The IP datagram format
The rules for resolving domain-name disputes
The 5G radio access network
questions.explain: RFC 791 defines the IP datagram format: 32-bit-wide rows holding fields such as version, header length, TTL, upper-layer protocol, header checksum, source and destination IP addresses, options and the payload.

questions.q: What is the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP)?
choices: A UN agency founded in 1865 for telegraph standards
An alliance of 7 global telecommunications standards groups that sets the technical specifications for 3G, 4G (LTE) and 5G cellular networks
A non-profit that assigns domain names
The IEEE committee responsible for Ethernet
questions.explain: 3GPP is an alliance of seven standards bodies (with about 745 member companies), so it is a kind of meta standards body. Its specifications come in "releases" spanning 3G, 4G and 5G.

questions.q: 3GPP's working groups are organized into which three technical areas?
choices: Radio access network
Service and systems aspects
Core network and terminals (end systems)
Domain name dispute resolution
Content filtering policy
questions.explain: 3GPP's 16 working groups fall into three areas: the radio access network, service/systems aspects, and the core network and terminals. Name disputes and content policy aren't part of its work.

questions.q: In the timeline of mobile cellular generations, which generation is characterized by broadband, end-to-end IP?
choices: 1G
2G
3G
4G
questions.explain: 1G (1979) was analog mobile, 2G (1991) added text messaging, 3G (1998) brought Internet connectivity, 4G (2008) brought broadband end-to-end IP, and 5G (2019) targets high data rates, IoT, cloud and SDN.

questions.q: Which mobile cellular generation was analog, before networks went fully digital?
choices: 1G
2G
3G
5G
questions.explain: 1G (1979) was analog mobile phones. Later generations were digital: 2G added text messaging, and Internet connectivity came with 3G and later.

questions.q: Which pairing of IEEE standard families is correct?
choices: 802.3 = wired Ethernet; 802.11 = Wi-Fi wireless
802.3 = Wi-Fi wireless; 802.11 = wired Ethernet
questions.explain: IEEE, the professional organization for electrical engineers, has a standards subgroup (in which industry typically takes part) that manages 802.3 (wired Ethernet) and 802.11 (Wi-Fi), both link-layer standards.

questions.q: Which statement about the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) is accurate?
choices: It was founded in 1998 to internationalize Internet naming
It was formed in 1865 for telegraph and landline phone standards, has been a United Nations agency since 1949, and is the oldest of the networking standards bodies
It writes the RFCs that define TCP and IP
It is the alliance that sets 3G/4G/5G specifications
questions.explain: The ITU dates to 1865 (not a typo). It sets telegraph and landline phone network standards, became a UN agency in 1949, and has 193 member countries plus about 900 companies.

questions.q: The ITU is in the lead for setting Internet and mobile cellular networking standards.
questions.explain: Despite its age and size, the ITU is not in the lead for the Internet (the IETF is) or for mobile cellular networking (3GPP is).

questions.q: What does ICANN stand for?
choices: International Council for Addressing and Naming Networks
Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers
Internet Committee for Allocated Network Numbers
Institute for Computer and Network Naming
questions.explain: ICANN is the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, the non-profit, multistakeholder organization in charge of the names-and-numbers layer.

questions.q: Which of these are ICANN's roles?
choices: Assigning and adjudicating Internet names
Assigning Internet addresses to names and managing translation between names and addresses
Writing the RFCs that define TCP
Deciding what content may be posted online
Setting the Wi-Fi link-layer standard
questions.explain: ICANN has two main roles: it handles Internet names (assigning them and settling disputes), and it assigns addresses and manages name-to-address translation, which the Domain Name System performs. RFCs come from the IETF, Wi-Fi from IEEE, and ICANN doesn't regulate content.

questions.q: What does the question of who should own names ending in .PATAGONIA illustrate?
choices: That domain names are assigned at random
That naming can be murky: the name could reasonably belong to the outdoor-clothing company or to the region in South America, and ICANN has rules for such conflicts
That only governments may own top-level names
That IP addresses run out faster than names
questions.explain: Some assignments are obvious (www.umass.edu to UMass Amherst, apple.com to Apple), but others are contested. ICANN has rules for resolving these potential naming conflicts.

questions.q: Someone registers a domain such as JimKuroseIsAFlamingIdiot.com. What ICANN mechanism lets the targeted person challenge this abusive registration?
choices: The Uniform Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy
Filing an RFC with the IETF
Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act
A firewall rule at the national boundary
questions.explain: ICANN's Uniform Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy covers abusive domain name registrations, whether or not the name happens to be true.

questions.q: The 2019 sale of the domain name voice.com for $30 million illustrates what point?
choices: Domain names are worthless once a site is built
Names matter and can be very valuable, which raises the stakes of who assigns them and how disputes are settled
ICANN sets the price of every domain name
IP addresses are worth more than names
questions.explain: "Names are important!" Owning a domain name can be worth a great deal, which is part of why name assignment is a governance issue and not only a technical one.

questions.q: What system translates a host name such as gaia.cs.umass.edu into an IP address such as 128.119.40.186?
questions.explain: The Domain Name System (DNS) performs the worldwide name-to-address translation, which ICANN manages.

questions.q: Why was ICANN founded in 1998?
choices: To internationalize Internet naming and addressing, which had previously been overseen by the U.S. government
To replace the IETF as the Internet's protocol standards body
To give the United Nations direct control of domain names
To set standards for cellular networks
questions.explain: Before ICANN, the U.S. government oversaw Internet naming and addressing. ICANN was created as a non-profit to internationalize that role.

questions.q: In ICANN's processes, governments have a greater voice than businesses, academics and civil society.
questions.explain: ICANN's process is bottom-up, consensus-based and multistakeholder. Governments have an equal voice with businesses, academics and civil society, for example on advisory committees.

questions.q: How does ICANN reach its final decisions?
choices: Member countries vote, one vote per country, as in the UN model
The U.S. government approves every decision
The Board, advised by four committees, makes final decisions after multiple public postings, reviews and discussion, and its meetings are open so anyone can address it
IETF working groups decide based on running code
questions.explain: ICANN's meetings are open and anyone can address the Board, which contrasts with the UN model. The Board makes final decisions with advice from four committees and only after public postings, reviews and discussion.

questions.q: At the 2012 World Conference on International Telecommunications (WCIT), several countries proposed that "Member States [countries] shall have equal rights to manage the Internet." What would this have meant, and what happened to it?
choices: It would have strengthened ICANN's multistakeholder model, and it passed
It argued for government supremacy in Internet control without mentioning other stakeholders, moving away from ICANN's multistakeholder approach, and it did not pass
It would have handed domain naming to the IETF, and it passed
It would have banned national firewalls, and it did not pass
questions.explain: The proposal (from Russia, the UAE, China, Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Sudan and Egypt) reflects growing pressure from some to give governments the upper hand. It mentioned no other voices and was proposed but not passed.

questions.q: What is the role of the Internet Governance Forum (IGF), first convened by the UN Secretary-General in 2006 and renewed in 2015?
choices: It makes binding Internet content policy for UN member states
It assigns domain names and IP addresses
It is a forum for multistakeholder policy dialogue that does not make decisions but "informs and inspires those who do"
It writes technical standards for cellular networks
questions.explain: The IGF deliberates and does not decide. Unlike ICANN, or governments setting policy within their borders, it exists to inform and inspire the people who do make decisions.

questions.q: The Internet Governance Forum is a decision-making body whose rulings on Internet content are binding on its participants.
questions.explain: The IGF explicitly does not make decisions. It is a deliberation body for multistakeholder policy dialogue.

questions.q: Which three sets of players play a significant role in governing Internet content and access to it?
choices: The Internet Governance Forum (IGF)
Companies and organizations that produce and disseminate content (platforms, content producers)
National (and sometimes local) governments
IEEE 802 standards committees
3GPP working groups
questions.explain: The content-layer players are the IGF, content companies and platforms (such as Google, Facebook, Amazon, Netflix, Reddit and CNN), and governments. IEEE and 3GPP set infrastructure standards.

questions.q: A user posts a false, damaging claim about someone on a discussion website. Under the text of Section 230 (47 U.S.C. § 230), how is the website treated with respect to that post?
choices: As the publisher of the post, just like a newspaper that printed it
As the speaker of the post, because it hosted it
It is not treated as the publisher or speaker of the post, because the information came from another content provider (the user)
Section 230 applies only to ISPs, not to websites
questions.explain: Section 230 says: "No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider." This gives website platforms immunity with respect to third-party content.

questions.q: Section 230, which gives U.S. website platforms immunity with respect to third-party content, is part of which U.S. law?
questions.explain: Section 230 (47 U.S.C. § 230) is part of the U.S. Communications Decency Act.

questions.q: How do U.S. website platforms compare with traditional media when it comes to controlling content?
choices: Platforms have no influence on what users experience
Like traditional media, they control what you experience, but U.S. law treats them differently: Section 230 means they aren't treated as the publisher of third-party content
They are legally identical to newspapers in every respect
Only governments, never platforms, decide what users see
questions.explain: Millions of websites and services control what you experience, in some ways no differently than traditional media. In the U.S., though, there are important legal differences between traditional publishers and website platforms.

questions.q: A 2022 report described a Cambodian decree under which all web traffic would be routed through a government portal. Which governance layer and which kind of actor does this illustrate?
choices: Infrastructure layer; a standards body
Names and numbers; ICANN
Content layer; a national government controlling access to Internet content
Content layer; the Internet Governance Forum
questions.explain: National governments set laws within their jurisdictions, and some act to control access to the Internet or to its content. Other examples include Russia's moves toward Internet control and Vietnam's cybersecurity law.

questions.q: How does a firewall differ from an ordinary router or switch?
choices: It can be programmed with blocking rules as well as forwarding rules
It only forwards packets and cannot drop them
It assigns domain names to hosts
It works only inside home networks
questions.explain: A firewall is a mechanism for controlling content access through programmable rules. Besides forwarding, it can drop packets that match a rule.

questions.q: A firewall at a national boundary is programmed with the rule "do not forward any packets with destination IP address 128.119.40.186." What is the effect?
choices: Users inside the boundary who use that network can no longer reach content at that address, because their packets are dropped at the firewall
The server at that address is shut down
Only packets containing a particular phrase are dropped
Users outside the country can no longer reach the server
questions.explain: The firewall drops packets headed to that destination address. Every user inside the national boundary whose traffic passes through it is cut off from that content. The server itself keeps running and remains reachable from elsewhere.

questions.q: What does a firewall doing deep packet inspection do?
choices: Checks only the destination IP address in the header
Looks inside a packet and decides whether to forward it based on its content, e.g., "don't forward any packets containing the phrase X"
Encrypts packets so they can't be read
Translates host names into IP addresses
questions.explain: Address-based rules look only at where a packet is going. Deep packet inspection examines what the packet carries and filters on that content.

questions.q: A national firewall drops every packet whose destination IP address is 128.119.40.186. The same content is also replicated on a server outside the country at a different IP address. What happens when a user inside the boundary requests the replica?
choices: The packets are dropped, because the firewall recognizes the content is identical
The rule doesn't match the replica's address, so the packets are forwarded and the user can reach the content
All traffic leaving the country is automatically blocked
The replica's address is automatically added to the blocking rule
questions.explain: An address-based rule matches only the address it names. Blocking the replica would need another rule for its address, or a content-based rule using deep packet inspection.
